1:
Boaz is introduced by his wealth; they fill out the rest. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that the Chaldee renders the phrase mighty in the law, and that if he was both it was a rare conjunction, to be mighty in wealth and mighty in the scriptures too; he adds that the man carries might in his very name. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) supplies the pedigree and its difficulty: by the line given at the close of the book Boaz is grandson of the Nahshon who was prince of the tribe of Judah during the wanderings, and son of Salmon and Rahab of Jericho, which crowds the generations — a difficulty he thinks eased by supposing the last two to be children of their fathers’ old age, any gaps belonging rather to the genealogy’s earlier portion.

That nobody helped the widows is noticed, and pressed. John Gill (reformed) finds it strange on both sides: Naomi made no application to a kinsman well known to her, which might arise from modesty and a reluctance to trouble a relation of her husband’s rather than her own; and stranger still, the kinsman took no notice of her, generous though he was, and though he had heard Ruth’s character — unless he was simply not acquainted with their indigent circumstances. Henry turns it on the town: the Bethlehemites would have done well to invite the two first to one good house and then to another, but instead of tasting the dainties of Canaan they had no way of getting necessary food but by gleaning, and might have starved — God has chosen the poor of this world, and poor they are likely to be, for though God has chosen them men commonly overlook them.

The right to glean is set out, then qualified. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) explain that the Mosaic law expressly secured the poor their gleaning and forbade owners to glean their own fields, but that hard-hearted farmers and reapers obstructed the poor and even forbade them altogether, which is why Ruth proposed to glean after whoever should generously allow it. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) confirms the fragility of such a right from nearer home: the practice was long a general custom in England and Ireland, supposed to be a right recognised by law — but it is now settled by a solemn judgment of the court of common pleas that no right to glean can be claimed at common law, any man being free to permit or prevent it in his own ground, while Irish statutes have restricted it so far as to prohibit it. Ruth’s phrasing, he adds, seems to intimate that notwithstanding the law of Moses the gleaners might be prevented by the owner. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads her phrasing as modesty rather than doubt, that though it was their duty to permit this she thought it might perhaps be denied her.

How she came to that field is the one point on which all agree, and each puts it differently. Keil and Delitzsch give the Hebrew bluntly, that her chance chanced to hit upon the field, she knowing neither the owner nor his connection with Elimelech. Clarke sets the two words side by side, that she was accidentally or providentially led to that part of the country which belonged to Boaz. Ellicott will not leave them so: her hap happened, he grants, a chance in outward seeming, yet a clear shaping of her course by unseen hands, her steps divinely guided to a certain field that God’s purposes should be worked out. Wesley makes the distinction a rule: a chance in reference to second causes but ordered by God’s providence, since God wisely orders small events, and many a great affair is brought about by a little turn, fortuitous as to men but designed by God.
4:
The greeting in the field is admired, and once qualified. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls it worthy of particular regard, and asks whether a pious mind can read such godly salutations without wishing for a return of those simple primitive times. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads it as evidence of a household in good order: Boaz did not fall a chiding them as if he came only to find fault, but prayed for them, and they did not, once he was out of hearing, fall a cursing him, as ill-natured servants do who hate their master’s eye — things go well in a house where there is such good-will. But Henry alone adds a caution, that such pious ejaculations must not degenerate into formality, lest in them we take the name of the Lord our God in vain.

The owner coming out to his own harvest draws one proverb from several sources. Henry puts it bluntly, that he who wholly leaves his business to others will have it done by the halves, since the master’s eye makes a fat horse; and he turns it to charity, that masters who live at ease should think tenderly of those who bear the burden and heat of the day. John Gill (reformed) gathers the same saying from the ancients: Pliny reports it as an old proverb that the eye of the master is the most fruitful thing in the field, and Aristotle tells of a Persian asked what most fattened a horse who answered, the eye of the master. Clarke finds the whole scene on the shield of Achilles, where the man in charge is called king and his staff a sceptre and stands in mute dignity to see the work well done — and where, he thinks, there are gleaners too, in the boys who gather after the binders.

The blessing Boaz pronounces is traced to its sources, and its central figure disputed. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hear the patriarch behind it: in leaving father and mother and the land of her nativity for a people she knew not, Ruth had done what God commanded Abraham, the full reward Boaz wishes her recalls the promise made to Abraham, and the sheltering wings come from the song of Moses — words showing, they say, the genuine piety of a true Israelite. Clarke takes the wings from the young of fowls, which on sighting a bird of prey run to their mother to be covered, and shelter so from storms; he infers that Ruth had already attached herself to the Jewish religion. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) allows that figure but sets another beside it, the wings of the Cherubim between which God dwelt.

Her answer is read for its self-abasement, the meal for its detail. Clarke explains that she prostrated herself as inferiors did in the East before superiors, and reports the Targum’s expansion, where Ruth asks how she has found grace, being a daughter of Moab, of whom it is said that the unclean shall not enter the congregation; Boaz answers that the decree touched the men and not the women, and that prophecy had promised kings and prophets from her. Keil and Delitzsch catch how she takes her own words back, having called herself his maiden and then adding that she is not like one of them — what am I saying, an older commentator glossed, when I call myself thy maiden, being unworthy to be compared with the least? Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that her foreignness was less of a barrier than it sounds, the Moabite tongue differing little from Hebrew as King Mesha’s inscription shows. On the dish they differ: Keil and Delitzsch make the chomez a sour drink of vinegar and oil, where Clarke takes it for an acid sauce the reapers dipped bread in.
17:
The day’s work and its yield are measured. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notices how little she took of what was offered: though Boaz had ordered handfuls left for her she went on gleaning the scattered ears, and scarcely used, much less abused, his kindness. She gleaned until evening, making no excuse to go home early; she threshed the corn herself to carry it the more easily; and she carried it into the city herself, though the servants would likely have done it had she asked — for we should study to be as little troublesome as may be to those who are kind to us. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) gives the same reason for the threshing, that it saved her the labour of carrying away the straw, and reckons the ephah at rather more than four pecks, where Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts it at seven gallons and a half and calls it a good day’s work.

The homecoming is read for what it shows of the household. Henry marks that she went straight home without staying to talk with the servants, and showed her mother-in-law what she had gleaned so that Naomi might see she had not been idle: having shown industry abroad, she showed piety at home. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) fasten on the odd verb, that she drew out — from her pocket, as the Chaldee rightly supplies — what she had left over from her sufficiency, meaning the parched corn Boaz had reached her at the meal. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) makes the same connection in four words, that what she reserved was from the dinner, after she had eaten and was sufficed.

Naomi infers a benefactor before she is told of one, and her blessing turns out to be ambiguous. Keil and Delitzsch have her reason from the evidence, conjecturing from the quantity of barley and the food brought home that someone had taken notice of Ruth, and then, on hearing the name, seeing that this relative had been chosen by God to be a benefactor to them both. Ellicott raises a difficulty the others pass over: it is not clear whether the one who has not left off his kindness to the living and the dead is God or Boaz, though either way a good sense is obtained. If it is Boaz, he finds it curious that Naomi, knowing she lived near a kinsman who had shown kindness before they went to Moab, had never made herself known to him — a proof, he says, of the independence of her character. Clarke identifies the parties plainly, that Naomi and Ruth were the living and also the representatives of Elimelech and Mahlon, who were dead.

The word kinsman is then unpacked, and the chapter closes on a waiting. Clarke explains the term as one of our redeemers, a near kinsman with the right to redeem a forfeited inheritance, and sets out the threefold office: to buy back the inheritance or the liberty of one who had sold himself for a servant, to avenge the blood of a murdered relative, and to take the widow of a kinsman who died childless — a nearest kinsman who refused being treated with indignity and losing his right. Ellicott renders the phrase as one of those who must redeem, and observes that the name once named sets going the train of thought that at length leads Naomi to appeal to him for a redeemer’s aid. Keil and Delitzsch explain Naomi’s satisfaction, since Ruth would be secured from the insults she might meet gleaning in strange fields; and they hear in the closing remark that she dwelt with her mother-in-law a tacit allusion to the change that came once the harvest was over. John Gill (reformed) sums her conduct through it all as a wonderful instance of dutiful affection, humility and industry.
